nameStory: The Siberian Crane's-bill gets its name from its homeland across the vast steppes and forests of Siberia in northern Asia. Like all crane's-bills, it's named for its distinctive seed pod that looks remarkably like a crane's long, pointed beak - when the seeds are ripe, this 'beak' splits open and catapults the seeds away from the parent plant!
description: Siberian Crane's-bill is a low-growing perennial wildflower that forms spreading mats close to the ground. This hardy little plant produces small, delicate pink or white flowers with five rounded petals throughout the growing season. Its deeply divided, palm-shaped leaves are soft and somewhat fuzzy to the touch, giving the whole plant a gentle, cottage-garden appearance despite its tough, cold-climate origins.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small five-petaled flowers in soft pink or white, about half an inch across, with delicate purple veins running through the petals that feel papery-thin when touched gently

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided palm-shaped leaves that feel soft and slightly fuzzy, cut into 5-7 narrow finger-like segments that give them an almost fern-like delicacy

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Long, pointed seed pods that look like a crane's bill, about an inch long, that split dramatically when ripe to fling seeds several feet away

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, spreading perennial that hugs the ground and forms loose mats, rarely getting taller than 8-12 inches even when flowering

habitat: With only one recorded observation in New England, Siberian Crane's-bill is extremely rare in our region and likely represents an escaped garden plant or accidental introduction. In its native range, it thrives in disturbed soils, roadsides, and open areas with good drainage. If found here, it would most likely be near gardens, parks, or areas where seeds might have been accidentally introduced.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge early, forming fresh green mats of soft, divided foliage that feels almost velvety to the touch.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering time with small pink or white blossoms appearing continuously through the warm months, followed by the characteristic crane's-bill seed pods.
seasonality.fall: Late flowers may still appear while earlier seed pods are splitting open with audible little 'pops' on dry days, flinging seeds in all directions.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving only dried stems and scattered seeds as evidence of its presence.

funFact: The seed pods of crane's-bills are like tiny botanical catapults - when they dry out, they suddenly coil and snap, launching seeds up to 20 feet away with enough force that you can actually hear them hit nearby leaves!
confusionNotes: With only one sighting in New England, you're much more likely to encounter our native Wild Geranium, which has larger, more deeply colored pink-purple flowers and grows much taller. Siberian Crane's-bill stays low and mat-forming with much smaller, paler flowers.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse wild geraniums (crane's-bills) with the colorful geraniums sold at garden centers - those are actually pelargoniums from South Africa! True geraniums are the humble wild crane's-bills with their characteristic beak-like seed pods.
compareHints: Among New England's crane's-bills, Siberian Crane's-bill would be one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species. Unlike our tall native Wild Geranium with its showy purple-pink flowers, or the sprawling red-stemmed Herb Robert, Siberian Crane's-bill stays very low to the ground with tiny, pale flowers that seem almost miniature compared to its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild geranium stands out from its cranesbill cousins by its substantial size, soft pink flowers, and preference for rich woodlands.
Among New England's wild geraniums, Herb Robert is the most delicate and lacy-looking, with much more finely divided leaves than the larger Wild Geranium.
Among New England's crane's-bills, bloody crane's-bill stands out for its deeply divided leaves that are cut almost to the base, creating very narrow segments.
Among New England's crane's-bills, rock crane's-bill is unique for its low, mat-forming growth and intensely fragrant leaves - most others grow more upright and have much less scented foliage.
Northern cranesbill is much smaller and more delicate than wild geranium, with tiny lavender flowers instead of large pink ones.
Thunberg's Geranium is much smaller and more delicate than our common Wild Geranium, with more finely divided leaves and smaller flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Carolina crane's-bill has the smallest flowers - much tinier than the showy inch-wide blooms of wild geranium or the medium-sized flowers of Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, meadow crane's-bill is one of the largest and most robust, forming much bigger clumps than most relatives.

Among New England's crane's-bills, dusky crane's-bill is unique for its nearly black flowers with backward-curved petals - our native wild geranium has pink flowers that face upward, while Herb Robert has small bright pink flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, dove's-foot stands out for its exceptionally soft, velvety leaf texture and low, mat-forming growth habit.
Among New England's crane's-bills, this is one of the tiniest and most easily overlooked.
Purple-vein geranium stands out from other New England geraniums primarily by its bright blue flowers - most other species have pink, white, or purple blooms.

Among New England's crane's-bills, cut-leaved crane's-bill stands out for having the most finely divided leaves - while wild geranium has broader, less deeply cut leaves and Herb Robert has more triangular leaf segments, cut-leaved crane's-bill looks almost feathery.
Among New England's crane's-bills, little-robin is the tiniest - much smaller than wild geranium or Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Long-stalked stands out for its exceptionally long flower stalks and deeply dissected leaves.

Richardson's geranium differs from New England's common wild geranium by having paler flowers with more prominent dark veining, perfectly straight (not curved) seed beaks, and more finely divided leaf segments.
Wood crane's-bill differs from our native wild geranium by having more deeply dissected leaves and typically stronger purple coloring with more prominent petal veining.
